item.title: Kyla Scanlon Launches Podcast 'Best of Luck' with Vox
item.description:
Source: Vox Original headline: Bestselling Author and Economic Commentator Kyla Scanlon Launches Weekly Podcast, ‘Best of Luck,’ with Vox
Kyla Scanlon, bestselling author and economic commentator, and Vox launched the weekly podcast 'Best of Luck,' premiering October 27. The show features interviews with professionals across fields, exploring career-building strategies in today’s economy. Scanlon emphasizes that traditional career advice is outdated, with guests sharing detours, setbacks, and successes. Each episode includes mock job interviews and advice autopsies, offering practical insights for navigating modern work life. Scanlon, known for her accessible economic analysis and term 'vibecession,' aims to connect complex economic concepts to everyday experiences. Vox’s editor-in-chief praised her ability to explain the economy in relatable terms, while the podcast joins Vox’s existing popular shows. Scanlon’s work includes a New York Times bestseller and contributions to CNN and The New York Times Opinion. The podcast will be available on major platforms, expanding Vox’s reach in explanatory content.

item.title: North Korea Releases Photos of Kim Jong Un Amid Death Rumors
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: North Korea publishes photos of Kim Jong Un - why do rumours of his death keep coming back?
North Korea released photos of Kim Jong Un appearing healthy at a clothing exhibition, contradicting claims he died from a brain hemorrhage. Chinese dissident Wanjun Xie alleged Kim was hospitalized in Beijing in a coma and later died, but no evidence supports this. Such rumors are common in North Korea, where information is tightly controlled. Xie, a banned Chinese political group member, previously spread unverified claims about Chinese leaders. Kim's health risks, including obesity and smoking, and family history of cardiovascular issues, make his condition a concern. Intelligence agencies warn of potential instability if Kim's health deteriorates, affecting North Korea's nuclear control and regional security. Succession uncertainty also fuels speculation, as Kim's daughter, 13 years old, has increasingly appeared in public but is not officially designated heir. The regime may intentionally obscure internal affairs, making verification difficult. Xie's claim highlights how misinformation thrives in North Korea's secrecy, with no confirmed evidence of Kim's death despite repeated rumors.

item.title: Sudan Army Drones Kill Over 300 in Funeral and Market Strikes
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
Sudan's army drones struck mourners and a fuel market, killing over 300 people, according to sources. Attacks in West Kordofan state on Sunday evening killed 150, with 145 fatalities from a drone strike on a funeral procession and 15 more from a market hit. Abyei, a disputed border area, saw 153 deaths when drones bombed a market on Monday, per the region's information minister. The army claimed the market was a RSF fuel supply site. The strikes have escalated tensions between Sudan and South Sudan, which both claim Abyei. UN officials condemned the attacks, noting they disrupted essential services and worsened a humanitarian crisis affecting 20 million people. Market traders described the destruction, with one stating the attack caused massive fires and material damage. Medical teams reported over 20 injured, including critical cases, at a hospital in Abyei. Drones also struck near Khartoum's airport, killing four, including children. The conflict, now in its second year, has intensified as the army regains control of strategic regions rich in resources.

item.title: Kenya Cult Leader's Children Still Starved Weeks Before Trial, Son Says
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Kenya cult leader's children still being starved weeks before trial, son says
Dan Mackenzie, son of Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie, claims his younger siblings were still forced to fast as recently as two weeks before his father's trial. Police rescued eight children, including his five siblings, from their grandmother's home after Dan reported the abuse. Paul Mackenzie was convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult in Shakahola forest, where he ordered followers to starve themselves to 'meet Jesus.' Twenty-eight cult leaders were also convicted. Dan, who initially defended his father, now works as a motorcycle taxi driver in Malindi, supporting his siblings. He described childhood abuse, including forced fasting and beatings. Justice Diana Mochache noted the cult's belief that Paul Mackenzie was 'Jesus's mouthpiece' and that resistance to fasting required 'kicks and blows.' The verdict was welcomed by victims' families, including Stephen Mwiti, who lost all six of his children. Mackenzie faces separate terrorism and education denial charges. The murder conviction is the first ruling against him, with sentencing scheduled for November 6. The trial followed the 2023 discovery of over 400 bodies in Shakahola forest.

item.title: Brother of the More Famous Jack Reaches New Readers
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Culture Original headline: 'Brother of the More Famous Jack' finds its way to a new generation of readers
Barbara Trapido's 1982 novel 'Brother of the More Famous Jack' has been reissued by New York Review Books' Classics imprint in October. The latest edition features a misleading cover photo evoking 1980s melancholy instead of the novel's 1960s London setting. The coming-of-age story follows Katherine Browne, a young woman navigating a chaotic philosophy professor's family, who becomes enamored with their radical lifestyle. Trapido's work explores themes of social class, sexual education, and intellectual eroticism, blending snappy dialogue with turbulent relationships. The novel, praised as 'literary comfort food' by Lily King and 'brilliantly lewd' by Rachel Cusk, contrasts with Trapido's later, bleaker works. Its title references poet William Butler Yeats, older brother of artist Jack Butler Yeats. The book's enduring appeal lies in its vivid portrayal of rebellion against bourgeois norms and its sharp, often raunchy humor.

item.title: U.S. and Ukraine Resume Intelligence Sharing Amid Diplomatic Talks with Russia
item.description:
Source: BBC News, Washington Post - World Original headline: U.S. and Ukraine Resume Intelligence Sharing as Diplomatic Talks Continue with Russia
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss peace proposals following talks in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Zelensky confirmed intelligence sharing with the U.S. on Russian missile attacks is functioning, countering earlier Kyiv claims of withheld information. The U.S. denied these allegations, calling them 'scandalous.' Zelensky praised improved early warning systems for civilian protection and reiterated Ukraine's readiness for negotiations, stressing Russia must accept Oslo-agreed terms. Finnish President Alexander Stubb noted 'genuine progress' on peace proposals but warned patience is needed. Jared Kushner joined the Oslo talks via video. Putin has not commented, but Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Russia will consider Witkoff's offer without 'political concessions.' U.S.-Ukraine relations remain strained, with Trump criticizing Kyiv's leadership and blaming Ukraine's attacks on Russian fuel prices. Russian drone attacks killed at least 10, including near Kharkiv. U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine was restored after restrictions linked to Trump's actions, though Kyiv alleged limited Starlink access and delayed missile deliveries. Zelensky raised concerns about Starlink speed restrictions impacting drone operations. A trilateral meeting between Trump, Zel, and Putin was discussed. Witkoff's meeting will also address securing the release of U.S. teacher Stephen Hubbard. Trump claimed Ukraine, not Russia, is blocking peace.

item.title: Toxic Haze Blankets Southeast Asia from Borneo Fires
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Borneo burning: Life on the frontline of South East Asia's toxic haze
Wildfires in Indonesian Borneo have blanketed Southeast Asia in toxic haze, burning 1.9 million hectares since January, with 1 million hectares burned in September alone. The smoke has caused severe health issues, including 277,000 reported cases of respiratory infections, with 62,000 affecting children under five. Mothers like Dianyra Eka Nastiti describe nightly fears for their children's health, while others like Lola Macitri report forced indoor confinement and disrupted schooling. Health officials warn of microparticles and carbon monoxide posing long-term risks, especially to children, elderly, and pregnant women. The government deployed 60,000 personnel to suppress fires, claiming an 80% success rate, but firefighters like Juni and Fauzi Rahman face challenges due to drought and water scarcity. Peatland fires require extensive water, which is increasingly hard to find. Experts like Dr. Nisa Novita note fires spreading into new areas, complicating efforts. Residents await rain to end the crisis, with officials expressing hope for divine intervention to bring relief.

item.title: AI Uses Facial Photos to Predict Cancer Survival Risk
item.description:
Source: Washington Post Original headline: How a photo of a patient’s face could predict whether they’ll survive cancer
Researchers developed FAHR-FaceSurvival, an AI model trained on 40 million facial photos to predict cancer mortality risk. Published in Lancet Digital Health, the system analyzes facial features to estimate biological age and survival outcomes. Among cancer patients, those in the top 10% FAHR-FaceSurvival scores had 50% mortality within 90 days, versus 2% in the lowest 10%. The model focuses on areas below the eyes and nasolabial folds, linking facial changes to physiological conditions. Raymond Mak, a Mass General Brigham oncologist, noted the system improves on earlier FaceAge technology by directly predicting mortality rather than just biological age. Critics like Suchi Saria and Emma Pierson raised concerns about bias and whether the model captures new biomarkers or existing clinical observations. The study excluded frailty measures and relied on data from high-income countries, prompting calls for broader validation. Mak emphasized the potential for low-cost facial imaging as a new biomarker source, calling it the start of a new medical field.

item.title: Five Grocery Items' Prices Fluctuate Due to Weather, Tariffs, and Disease
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: Why these 5 everyday items fluctuate in price at the grocery store
Grocery prices for five everyday items have fluctuated due to weather, tariffs, disease, and supply chain issues. Post-pandemic, food inflation slowed but remained elevated. Ground beef prices surged 85% since 2014 due to droughts, reduced cattle herds, and industry consolidation. Eggs spiked from $2.27 to $6.23 per dozen in 2023 amid avian flu outbreaks, which forced culling of flocks. Coffee prices rose 44% since 2022, driven by climate disruptions in Brazil, Vietnam, and Costa Rica, alongside Trump-era tariffs. Butter prices dropped 17.3% as U.S. production surged, outpacing demand. Chocolate chip cookies hit $5.35 per pound in 2023 due to high flour, cocoa, and egg costs, though prices eased slightly. Experts note inflation compounds existing high prices, with factors like labor costs and tariffs further straining retailers. Professor Ricky Volpe warned that current inflation builds on prior price hikes, making consumers more sensitive to cost increases.

item.title: Vanessa Kerry Appointed WHO Health Resilience Envoy
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: Vanessa Kerry is the new WHO envoy for health resilience. What's on her to-do list?
Vanessa Kerry has been appointed as WHO's special envoy for health resilience. She emphasizes preparedness through strong health systems, primary care, and response capabilities. Kerry, who previously served as WHO's climate change and health envoy, is also director of global and climate health policy at Harvard and founder of Seed Global Health, an organization training healthcare workers in low-resource countries since 2006. Her career was shaped by a harrowing labor delivery in Rwanda during medical school, where she and a nurse successfully delivered a baby despite lacking training. This experience led her to found Seed, which partners with governments to build sustainable healthcare infrastructure. In Uganda, Seed trained 30 emergency physicians and 3,000 health workers during an Ebola outbreak. Kerry argues that resilience requires investing in systems, not just crisis response, and insists on prioritizing local needs. 'Resilience means building a system that will already be in place,' she says, stressing the need for funding to address major health burdens effectively.

item.title: Rubio visits India to address global energy shortages
item.description:
Source: Washington Post - World Original headline: Rubio visits India seeking relief from global energy crunch
Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited India to address global energy shortages, focusing on refining Venezuelan crude at Reliance Industries' refinery. During talks with Indian Foreign Secretary S. Jaishankar, Rubio emphasized the facility's capacity to process heavy Venezuelan crude, which could ease market pressures. Reliance, owned by Mukesh Ambani, has ties to the Trump administration and is expanding its Texas refinery project. U.S.-India trade tensions persist due to Trump's tariffs, Pakistan outreach, and unresolved trade deals. Trump's pause on Russian oil sanctions eased India's energy concerns, as the country relies heavily on Russian imports amid Middle Eastern disruptions. Analysts note that while core ties remain, unresolved issues like tariffs and Pakistan outreach strain relations. Rubio's visit aimed to bolster business and security ties, with both sides expressing optimism despite ongoing challenges.

item.title: U.K. Police Rearrest Two in Suspected Iranian Air Base Plot
item.description:
Source: Washington Post - World Original headline: U.K. police rearrest two men in suspected Iranian plot on air base
British police rearrested two men suspected of involvement in a terrorism plot linked to Iran's security services targeting RAF Fairford, a U.S. air base. The suspects, a 24-year-old British national and a dual U.K.-Iranian national, were taken into custody under a national security act allowing prosecution for aiding foreign intelligence. The arrests followed a prior operation where five men were briefly detained after driving vans toward the base, prompting the U.S. to relocate B-1 bombers. Investigators found only gasoline cans in the vehicles, not weapons. Laurence Taylor, head of U.K. Counter Terrorism Policing, stated evidence suggests Iranian state involvement. Five other suspects remain on bail, including one who called emergency services after midnight, raising questions about the plot's intentions. Authorities continue to probe whether the plan involved arson or causing panic through vehicle attacks.

item.title: South African swimmer killed in shark attack off east coast
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Swimmer, 65, killed in shark attack off South Africa's east coast
A 65-year-old South African woman, Janine Lochrenberg, was killed in a shark attack off the east coast near KuGompo City on Tuesday. Witnesses reported she was bitten twice and died before being brought to shore. The attack occurred around 08:00 local time as she swam with her open water club. She had a magnetic shark repellent band on her ankle. Fellow swimmers described her injuries, including a bite to her thigh and upper arm. Her sister Margot said she bled out in the water, while her partner Barbara Briceland praised her bravery and intelligence. Lochrenberg, a retired medical physicist, often swam far out into the breakers. Authorities closed Orient Beach and a nearby beach following the incident. Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal cases since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File.

item.title: J. Crew Website Down with 'AI Backend Healthy' Message
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: J. Crew's website went down — and an odd message said its 'generative AI backend' was 'healthy'
J. Crew's website crashed Monday, displaying a message stating its 'generative AI backend' was 'healthy' on an otherwise blank page. Customers shared screenshots on social media expressing confusion, with one user asking, 'Wtf is up with the @jcrew website.' The brand's customer service account responded, apologizing and stating they were working to restore the site. Later, J. Crew emailed customers a 20% discount code expiring Thursday, thanking them for patience during the technical issues. The cause of the outage remains unclear, with J. Crew representatives not immediately commenting on the incident.

item.title: AI Bubble Burst Could Trigger Recession and Job Losses
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: What if an AI bubble bursts — and that accelerates AI job losses?
An AI bubble burst could trigger a recession, accelerating job losses through automation. J.P. Morgan found 42 AI-related companies accounted for two-thirds of the S&P 500's stock price gains since early 2024, while these firms borrowed hundreds of billions to fund data centers. Economist Charles Kindleberger's theory on financial bubbles warns that revolutionary technologies can fuel speculative frenzies, as seen with railroads in the 1870s. A 2024 study by Nir Jaimovich and Henry Siu found 88% of automation-driven job losses between 1990-2017 occurred during or near recessions. Technology analyst Benedict Evans warned that fierce AI competition could drive down profits, while cheaper AI tools might hasten worker replacement during economic downturns. A recession triggered by an AI bust could worsen job losses, creating a 'nightmare scenario' where investors lose money and workers face permanent unemployment. Policies like AI taxation and expanded unemployment insurance could mitigate impacts, though outcomes remain uncertain.

item.title: TikTok Executives Ignored Child Safety Concerns, Court Records Show
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: TikTok staff raised child safety alarms. Court records show executives failed to act
TikTok employees raised concerns about child safety risks, including sexual exploitation and exposure to harmful content, but executives failed to act, according to court records. Depositions from March 2026 reveal staff repeatedly warned about minors appearing in sexual content, bypassing age restrictions, and financial incentives for such content. Reagen Maher, a former senior safety executive, testified that leadership downplayed these risks, with internal chats showing she fought to address them for months. TikTok also avoided age verification surveys to prevent sharing data with the FTC. The company has settled multiple lawsuits, including a $100 million Alabama case over alleged addictive design and harmful content. Legal experts warn TikTok could face criminal liability for profiting from child exploitation via its gifting system, as federal law holds companies accountable for knowingly benefiting from such activities. TikTok did not respond to NPR's questions about reporting child sexual abuse material to NCMEC or handling revenue from illegal content. Employees highlighted a loophole allowing underage users to access adult features via third-party logins, which the company acknowledged internally but did not address. The app remains widely used, with 68% of U.S. teens ages 13-17 using it in 2025.

item.title: Kenya Confirms Nine Ebola Cases, Faces Spread Concerns
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
Kenya has confirmed nine Ebola cases, marking its first outbreak. The first patient, who died two weeks ago after traveling from DR Congo, infected four relatives, three health workers, and a hospital cleaner. Concerns about spread persist despite government reassurances. The Bundibugyo strain, with no approved vaccine, poses a risk due to Kenya's role as a regional transport hub. Enhanced screening at airports and borders targets high-risk countries, with travelers required to complete digital forms and present QR codes. Over 9,500 DR Congo cases and 4,000 deaths highlight regional risks. The government has quarantined 134 contacts, with 99% traced, and established a dedicated lab for testing. Health workers face risks, with unions criticizing protective equipment shortages. Neighboring countries like Uganda, Somalia, and Ethiopia have tightened surveillance. The US and UK issued travel advisories, but no travel bans exist. Kenya remains open, urging calm and vigilance while addressing stigma and ensuring healthcare worker safety.

item.title: Current U.S. support for Ukraine looks very different than it did
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World
U.S. support for Ukraine has shifted under President Trump, according to former ambassador William Taylor. Compared to Biden's strong response to Russia's 2022 invasion, current aid has dropped by 95%, with critical munitions paperwork unsigned and financial support halted. Taylor noted the U.S. now provides minimal assistance, relying on NATO allies and European purchases. Trump's pro-Russian stance, including sanctions waivers and an oil deal, has raised concerns about undermining Ukraine. Taylor warned that while a complete cutoff is unlikely due to public and congressional support, the administration's influence has waned. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy emphasized the war's human cost, stressing that Ukraine cannot stop resisting Russian occupation. Taylor argued that Trump's attempts to negotiate with Russia risk failing, as Ukrainians refuse to surrender. The U.S. continues to supply military intelligence and Starlink, but the overall support structure has weakened significantly.

item.title: Vegan Restaurant Numbers Fall 21-25% in Key U.S. Cities
item.description:
Source: Vox Original headline: Where did all the vegan restaurants go?
Mad Rabbit Cafe in Madison, Wisconsin, closed this week, joining a national trend of declining vegan restaurants. Data from HappyCow shows a 21-25% drop in vegan eateries in New York, Los Angeles, and Portland from 2022 to late 2024. Notable closures include Modern Love and Candle in NYC, the Vegan Joint in LA, and Millennium in Oakland. As of 2025, HappyCow lists 1,509 U.S. vegan restaurants, down from 1,717 in October 2025. The closure of Mad Rabbit, which served popular tofu scrambles and crepes, highlights the struggle for mid-tier cities to sustain vegan dining. Owner Nate Anger cited the demanding time commitment as a factor. Vegan restaurants, once niche, have become cultural anchors, blending creativity with activism. Historically, places like Paris’s Foyer Végétalien (1923) aimed to grow the movement through hospitality. Modern eateries like Moosewood and Soul Vegetarian pioneered plant-based cuisine, influencing mainstream adoption. Despite closures, vegan dining remains vital for proving the viability of plant-based food, offering diverse flavors and experiences that challenge stereotypes about veganism. The decline raises questions about the movement’s sustainability and the role of restaurants as spaces for innovation and community.
